sources.title: Audrey Hepburn (Q42786) -- live-checked entity data confirms canonical English label 'Audrey Hepburn'; occupations recorded include film actress, dancer, and humanitarian/goodwill ambassador. Nationality was independently verified (not read directly off a P27 claim) -- see provenance notes on the GB-vs-GB+BE decision.

UNICEF Executive Director's Office internal record, 'UNICEF Audrey Hepburn bio as of January 1991' (External ID CF-HST-BIO-HEP, Expanded Number CF-RAD-USAA-DB01-2005-00000030), UNICEF's own institutional History Project archive (cf-hst.net). Fetched directly as a PDF and read in full (a genuine primary institutional document -- a dated internal biography sheet on UNICEF letterhead, not a retrospective press retelling). Documents, with specific dates, countries, and named officials: her March 1988 appointment as UNICEF Special Ambassador (Goodwill Ambassador from 1989) and immediate mission to drought-stricken Ethiopia (Eritrea and Tigray); an October 1988 mission to Venezuela and Ecuador; February 1989 visits to Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Mexico, including individual meetings with Guatemalan Vice-President Carpio Nicolle, Honduran President Azcona, and Salvadoran President Duarte; April 1989 Congressional testimony in Washington, D.C. at Hearings of the House Foreign Operations Sub-Committee and the House Select Sub-Committee on Hunger, and meetings with President and Mrs. Bush and members of Congress; an April 12-16, 1989 mission to Sudan for Operation Lifeline Sudan, including travel to rebel-held Southern Sudan to meet rebel leaders and visits to displaced-persons camps at Muglad and El Mereim; and an October 1989 mission to Australia, Thailand, and Bangladesh, among other dated activities through late 1990.

British Film Institute, 'The letter that made Audrey Hepburn a star' (BFI National Archive, 'Inside the Archive' series). Fetched and read live via browser. Reproduces and quotes director William Wyler's own dated letter (26 October 1951) to Thorold Dickinson, who had shot Hepburn's screen test for Roman Holiday at Wyler's specific instruction to run the camera on an unscripted personal interview after the scripted scenes, to gauge her natural screen presence. Wyler's letter calls the test 'a fine piece of work' and 'as good as any I've seen in a long time,' stating it gave him 'a good look at the girl's personality and charm, as well as her talent.'

Open Culture, 'Audrey Hepburn's Moving Screen Test for Roman Holiday (1953)'. Fetched and read live. Independent of the BFI feature (different publisher), corroborating the same screen test: shot by Thorold Dickinson at Pinewood Studio on 18 September 1951, with 'a thousand feet of film' devoted to an unscripted interview in which Hepburn discussed her wartime experience of the Allied raid on Arnhem and hiding in a cellar; quotes Dickinson's own assessment of the interview footage as 'a deeply moving thing,' and independently reproduces Wyler's reaction on viewing it in Rome ('She had everything I was looking for: charm, innocence and talent... She was absolutely enchanting').

Turner Classic Movies, 'Roman Holiday - Behind the Camera'. Fetched and read live. Independent film-history/press account of the Roman Holiday production and its reception, including Gregory Peck's own recollection ('Everyone on the set of Roman Holiday was in love with Audrey... I think it was the happiest experience I ever had on a movie set').

Encyclopedia.com, reproducing Gale's Encyclopedia of World Biography / Contemporary Theatre, Film and Television entry on Audrey Hepburn, whose bibliography cites Charles Higham, Audrey: The Life of Audrey Hepburn (1984) -- read via encyclopedia.com's full reproduction of the reference-encyclopedia article, not by directly reading Higham's original biography (which was not independently located and read this cycle; the underlying book is therefore not itself listed as a source). Documents her 1948 scholarship to Marie Rambert's ballet school in London, the specific, quoted assessment that she was 'a good worker and wonderful learner' but 'too tall' at five feet seven inches and 'years behind in her training,' and her subsequent shift into modeling and West End chorus-line work rather than abandoning performance entirely.

discipline.rationale: A specific, named formal training program, not an inference from her later on-screen poise. Hepburn won a scholarship to Marie Rambert's ballet school in London in 1948, where she was assessed as 'a good worker and wonderful learner' -- a specific, quoted evaluation of her work ethic during training, not an inference from her later fame (src_hepburn_encyclopedia_gale). Scored moderately rather than high because this claim is single-sourced via a tertiary reference encyclopedia that cites, but was not itself directly read for this cycle, Charles Higham's 1984 biography -- confidence is capped accordingly. This row deliberately excludes the frequently-repeated claim that wartime malnutrition explains her physical constitution or any personality trait; per this rubric's evidence discipline, no row here infers anything about her personality from her health or wartime hardship. The row scores only the documented behavioral fact -- sustained, evaluated formal training -- not its physical causes or effects.

adaptability.rationale: A specific, dated professional redirection following a concrete setback, not a general 'resilience' inference. Rambert directly told Hepburn that, given her height (five feet seven inches) and having started professional training 'years behind,' the status of prima ballerina was unattainable. Rather than abandoning performance, she moved into modeling work and West End chorus-line work, which led within a few years to a Broadway role (Gigi, 1951) and then Roman Holiday (1953) (src_hepburn_encyclopedia_gale). Scored at moderate confidence because it is single-sourced via the same tertiary reference article as the discipline row above; this is the same underlying career episode viewed through a different, specifically behavioral lens (redirection after a professional rejection, not the training itself), not a restatement of the same row.

ambiguity_tolerance.rationale: A specific, dated, unusually extensive evaluative situation, not an inference from her eventual stardom. For her 18 September 1951 Roman Holiday screen test at Pinewood, director Thorold Dickinson -- at William Wyler's specific request -- kept the camera running after the scripted scenes and devoted a full thousand-foot reel to an unscripted personal interview, during which Hepburn discussed her wartime experience of the Allied raid on Arnhem and hiding in a cellar with no script or prepared answers. Dickinson himself described the resulting footage as 'a deeply moving thing' (src_hepburn_openculture), and Wyler's own dated letter (26 October 1951) says the test gave him 'a good look at the girl's personality and charm, as well as her talent' (src_hepburn_bfi). Two independent sources (BFI's archive and Open Culture) corroborate the same specific, unscripted, extended evaluative episode. Scored as a documented instance of sustaining a compelling, coherent self-presentation in an open-ended, unstructured situation with real career stakes and no script to fall back on, rather than an inference from the outcome (getting the role) alone.

impact_motivation.rationale: A sustained, multi-year, densely dated pattern of field commitment, not an inference from her having accepted a ceremonial title. UNICEF's own internal record (a primary institutional document, not a retrospective press account) shows Hepburn undertaking field missions to Ethiopia (1988), Venezuela and Ecuador (October 1988), Turkey (April 1988), Guatemala/Honduras/El Salvador/Mexico (February 1989), Sudan (April 1989), Australia/Thailand/Bangladesh (October 1989), and Vietnam (November 1990), among further dated activity through her death in January 1993 -- essentially continuous field and advocacy work across at least five years, not a single trip or a handful of appearances (src_hepburn_unicef_archive). Scored just below the 85+ extreme-score band deliberately: while the density and duration of the documented record is real and unusual, it derives from a single institutional source (UNICEF's own archive), and this rubric requires multiple independently-documented instances to justify an extreme score even where a single source is unusually rich and specific.

risk_tolerance.rationale: A specific, dated, bounded incident involving genuine personal-safety exposure, not an inference from general humanitarian commitment. During her April 12-16, 1989 mission to Sudan for Operation Lifeline Sudan, Hepburn 'traveled the difficult roads to the rebel-held Southern Sudan, where she met with rebel leaders,' and visited camps for displaced persons at Muglad and El Mereim, in the midst of an active civil war and famine emergency -- a specific, dated act of entering a conflict zone and meeting an armed opposition faction, not merely visiting a supervised refugee camp (src_hepburn_unicef_archive). Scored as documented and kept out of the extreme band (single institutional source, one bounded trip) despite the clear risk-bearing content of the specific, dated itinerary.

persuasiveness.rationale: A specific, sustained advocacy-communication pattern with named, high-level interlocutors, not an inference from her celebrity status alone. In February 1989 she met individually with Guatemalan Vice-President Carpio Nicolle, Honduran President Azcona, and Salvadoran President Duarte 'for important sessions concerning programmes to benefit the children of Central America'; in April 1989 she testified at two U.S. House sub-committee hearings and met with President and Mrs. Bush and members of Congress; and after her first Ethiopia mission in 1988 she sustained a schedule of 'as many as fifteen print and broadcast interviews a day' across the U.S., Canada, Switzerland, Finland, West Germany, and Italy for several weeks (src_hepburn_unicef_archive). Scored as a documented, sustained pattern of direct persuasive engagement with specific named decision-makers and press, not a single speech or appearance; single-sourced to UNICEF's own archive, so held below the extreme band and at moderate rather than high confidence.

provenance.notes: Wikidata QID (Q42786) verified live before scoring: canonical label 'Audrey Hepburn'; P106 occupations include film actress, dancer, model, humanitarian, and goodwill ambassador. NATIONALITY DECISION, resolved by live research rather than assumed: Hepburn was born in Ixelles, Brussels, Belgium, to a British father (Joseph Victor Anthony Ruston) and a Dutch mother (Baroness Ella van Heemstra), but under both then-current Belgian nationality law (patrilineal, no birthright citizenship from mere birth on Belgian soil) and British nationality law of the time, she was British by descent from birth and never held Belgian citizenship -- confirmed via multiple independent secondary accounts of the specific legal mechanism, not assumed from her birthplace. nationalityCodes was therefore set to GB alone (not GB+BE), consistent with this repo's existing convention of coding contributors by citizenship rather than birthplace alone (e.g. agatha-christie.json, bertrand-russell.json use GB alone despite complex personal histories). regionCode set to western_europe per the research brief. EVIDENCE READ: five substantive, independently-read sources beyond Wikipedia/Wikidata orientation, spanning four mutually independent, non-self perspectives: UNICEF's own internal archival record (a primary institutional document dated January 1991, not a retrospective account); the British Film Institute's National Archive feature reproducing Wyler's original 1951 letter; Open Culture (independent press, corroborating the same screen test with an additional named quote from Thorold Dickinson); Turner Classic Movies (independent press); and Encyclopedia.com's reproduction of Gale's reference-encyclopedia entry (citing, but not replacing, Charles Higham's 1984 biography, which was not independently located and read this cycle -- flagged honestly rather than listed as if directly consulted). This clears the >=2-independent-perspective / >=1-non-self-behavioral-source bar comfortably; every source used is non-self. Three of six scored rows (impact_motivation, risk_tolerance, persuasiveness) draw on the single UNICEF archival document, which is unusually rich and specifically dated -- each row scores a genuinely distinct facet of that same underlying field record (sustained multi-year commitment; a specific bounded personal-risk incident in rebel-held Southern Sudan; a specific pattern of high-level persuasive engagement) rather than the same claim restated three times, and none was pushed into the 85+ extreme-score band precisely because it rests on one institutional source, however rich. No row infers any personality trait from her wartime childhood hardship, malnutrition, or later fatal illness (she died of appendiceal cancer in January 1993); the Rambert ballet rows score only the documented training/assessment/career-redirection behavior, explicitly excluding the commonly-repeated wartime-malnutrition explanation for her physique. Considered and declined to use: a widely-circulated 'I have a broken heart' Ethiopia quote and a Roman Holiday crying-scene anecdote about William Wyler yelling at her to produce tears on camera -- both recur across secondary web aggregation but could not be traced to a citable original source (biography, archive, or dated press report) within this cycle, so neither is used as scored evidence or listed as a source. Portrait: searched Wikimedia Commons for a genuinely public-domain Hepburn photograph, specifically avoiding the many copyrighted Golden-Age-Hollywood studio portraits the research brief warned about (several Hollywood-era files on Commons carry no clear PD rationale and were not used). Selected a 28 September 1989 press photograph by Rob Bogaerts for Anefo (Dutch national press photo agency), held by the Nationaal Archief and released under a live-verified CC0 Public Domain Dedication (confirmed via the Commons API, not assumed from the file name) -- an authentic period photograph from her UNICEF Danny Kaye Award hosting work, independently confirmed as one of her documented UNICEF-era activities in the UNICEF archival source above. Downloaded directly (3730x2469 original) and resized with PIL (Lanczos resampling) to a 1600px long edge (1600x1059), saved to public/portraits/audrey-hepburn-unicef-1989.jpg, and the saved file's real pixel dimensions were verified after resize.
